extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and journalists interested in wartime reporting and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: An overview of how wartime censorship systems operate across countries and what that implies for correspondents' reporting practices; includes examples (Britain, Germany, Soviet Russia, occupied territories) and consequences for news flow. Aimed at informing readers about press conditions during war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report what you can justify as facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters in the United States "are free to tell what they see and what they can justify as facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes factual, justifiable reporting as the core obligation of correspondents; contrasted with environments of fear or strict censorship. Implicit anti-pattern: reporting rumors or unverified claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality of reporters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard expectation that correspondents should maintain impartiality in coverage. This appears as a general normative statement about conduct in reporting despite wartime pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of military information useful to the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nearly all countries bar what they consider military information 'that might be useful to an enemy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries routinely restrict publication of tactical/operational military details. Journalists should expect and avoid disclosure of material judged by authorities to risk aiding the enemy; anti-pattern: publishing sensitive troop/attack details during operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of responsibility (Germany/Italy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Foreign correspondents are under a 'censorship of responsibility.' ... They are free to send what they wish but they must conform to official reports on air raids, and send the news only after the raid is over; they must refrain from untruthful, damaging attacks on the Nazi government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A system where reporters have broad freedom but are constrained to follow certain official lines on specific subjects (e.g., air raids) and to avoid disparaging or damaging accusations. Practical guidance: delay sensitive items until allowed and avoid content that provokes punitive censorship; example: U.S. reporters had "practically normal, peace-time facilities" yet faced these constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: State control through official news sources (Soviet model)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Soviet Russia "the press examines carefully all news dispatches but generally allows any published matter to be sent abroad even when it is highly critical of Soviet events or officials. Soviet censorship operates chiefly through government control of news at its source. 'TASS, the official agency, newspapers and press officials necessarily are the chief sources of information.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship can be exercised by monopolizing information at its origin rather than by blunt suppression of outbound dispatches; reporters should understand official agency dominance and the limits it places on independent sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of neutral-country channels to transmit dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: "Correspondents have unhampered telephone communication with neutral countries to transmit their dispatches."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct transmission is constrained, journalists rely on neutral intermediaries (e.g., Switzerland) to get copy out. Practical tip: establish reliable neutral contacts and routes for transmitting reports when operating under censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/pencil-method censorship in possessions and colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessions such as Hong Kong, Singapore, India, Egypt and others "use London's pencil method." Canada "trusts newspapers and reporters to comply."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonial/possession administrations often apply a lighter, editorial-review style ('pencil method') rather than absolute suppression; guidance implies knowing local administrative practices and expectations for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy in occupied countries and gradual loosening
rubrics_metrics.description: "Facts may be hidden in an occupied country when communications are cut but such secrecy arouses suspicions that often are worse than the truth and occupation authorities usually loosen their regulations as the lesser evil."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect initial opacity in occupied territories; however, prolonged secrecy tends to backfire and authorities may relax controls. Reporting strategy: be attentive to signals that restriction regimes are changing and to alternative sources that surface over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship breakdowns prompted by competing narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by British censorship softening after Germany gave a 'play-by-play' account of a big air raid and public protest forced censors to allow fuller reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy censorship can be undermined when opposing powers publish alternative accounts or when public protest arises; journalists and editors should be aware that public reaction and competing information sources can change censorship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting from occupied regions tends to be undramatic and gradual
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatches from German-occupied regions "generally are without dramatics. They deal with the ordinary life of average people," so knowledge of events "often seems less than it is because that news is obscured by" other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents should expect that reliable reporting from occupied areas often focuses on quotidian details and may understate the situation; guidance for readers/editors: value such reports for their steady accrual of evidence rather than sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: State theory: controlling newspapers to direct public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the theory of many governments that public opinion can be directed ... Where censorship is heavy, the public buys fewer newspapers, whether through distrust or economy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recognition that censorship is used as social control but has consequences for readership and trust. For news producers, this is a caution about the trade-offs of heavy information control and its effect on audience engagement.
